after.answer: My working position is that the town should adopt a two-pool rolling allocation with equal-chance lotteries for open slots plus a small bounded access reserve with automatic return of unclaimed reserve blocks and consecutive-loss carryover, a published rubric for milestone-based project priority, progressive release and standby filling of unused project blocks, and public adaptive review. In detail: divide each machine's bookable time into equal blocks each week. Reserve 60% of blocks for the Open Pool and 40% for the Project Pool, with the split published and adjustable only within a pre-announced range after review. The Open Pool is allocated by lottery: every resident gets one base ticket per block; a newcomer gets a one-time guaranteed first-use token and, for the first three bookings, one extra ticket; anyone who has not used the workshop in 90 days gets one extra ticket. To avoid repeated losses for urgent or schedule-constrained residents, 10% of Open Pool blocks are reserved for urgent/essential use and recurring schedule windows, allocated by lottery among eligible applicants. If fewer eligible residents claim the reserved blocks than are reserved, every unclaimed reserved block returns immediately to the general Open Pool draw for that block or, if the general draw has already occurred, to the standby instant-fill queue; no reserved block is held unused. The reserve is capped at 10% of Open Pool blocks and can be adjusted only between 5% and 15% after public review, with a rollback trigger if it raises non-urgent wait times or unused bookings beyond pre-announced bounds. Any resident who loses two consecutive Open Pool draws receives one priority ticket in the next draw. The Project Pool is for projects needing at least three blocks in a month. Applicants submit a one-page public plan, requested blocks, and milestones. A rotating resident-staff panel scores plans using a published rubric with objective indicators and anchors: feasibility (materials, skills, certification, time estimate), public benefit (residents served, open output, shared repair, teaching), and readiness (confirmed materials, training, prior milestones). Panel decisions must give written rubric-linked reasons, and priority expires after the project window and is not transferable. Experienced users can receive contiguous blocks, but unused Project Pool blocks are progressively released: milestone check and tentative release to the priority waitlist at 72 hours, firm release to the Open Pool at 24 hours, and a standby instant-fill queue at start; cancellations automatically promote the next waitlisted resident. No-shows without an accepted excuse lose one lottery ticket for 30 days, not permanent access. All weights, queues, scores, and reasons are posted in plain language. Any resident can challenge an allocation or rule: first a written review by an elected workshop council, then an appeal to a randomly selected resident panel with staff advice, with written reasons and a public log; challenges to scoring check rubric application. The town runs a six-month trial with pre-announced metrics—newcomer first-use rate, project completion rate, machine utilization, no-show rate, appeal outcomes, bounded access wait time, consecutive-loss rate, urgent-reserve use, unclaimed-reserve return rate, and release fill rate—and adjusts weights or split only within pre-set bounds after public review. This remains fair because newcomers have guaranteed and equal-chance access, urgent and schedule-constrained residents have bounded access with no wasted reserved capacity, experienced users get transparent rubric-based project priority rather than wealth or connections, and unused capacity is recycled. It remains useful under strategic booking because hoarding is costly, priority expires, no-shows are penalized mildly, release is progressive with standby fill, and public metrics plus challenge rights make capture or error visible and correctable.

claims.value: Adopt a two-pool rolling allocation with equal-chance Open Pool lotteries plus a bounded access reserve that returns unclaimed reserved blocks to the general draw or standby queue, consecutive-loss carryover, a published-rubric Project Pool, progressive release with standby filling, and public bounded adaptive review.

derivation_steps.statement: The problem asks for an allocation arrangement that simultaneously serves newcomer fairness, experienced-project completion, low unused bookings, and understandable/challengeable rules under unknown demand and strategic booking; this would be contradicted if a proposal could meet the problem while ignoring one of those four goals.

Pure first-come-first-served should not be the main allocator because it favors residents who can watch the queue and book early, which tends to reduce newcomer chances and invite strategic hoarding; this would be contradicted if a first-come-first-served scheme reliably gave newcomers equal access without hoarding or deadweight loss.

A single all-slot lottery gives equal chances but cannot reliably assemble the long contiguous blocks that demanding projects need, so the design needs a separate project pool; this would be contradicted if one all-slot lottery met project-completion needs without harming newcomer access or utilization.

A published split between an Open Pool and a Project Pool makes the fairness/usefulness trade-off explicit and reviewable; this would be contradicted if no stable split could be published or if any fixed split made one of the four goals impossible.

The Open Pool should use equal base lottery tickets plus a temporary newcomer or returning-user boost rather than permanent priority, because temporary boosts give newcomers a fair start without creating inherited advantage; to answer the peak-exclusion objection, the Open Pool also gets a small bounded access reserve for urgent/essential and recurring schedule-window use and a consecutive-loss carryover that gives a priority ticket after two unsuccessful draws. To answer the unclaimed-reserve objection, the reserve is capped at 10% of Open Pool blocks, can move only between 5% and 15% after public review, and any reserved block not claimed by an eligible resident returns immediately to the general Open Pool draw or to the standby queue; this would be contradicted if these bounded-access additions failed to improve access for urgent or schedule-constrained residents without crowding out newcomers or increasing unused bookings, or if unclaimed reserved blocks were held rather than returned.

Project Pool access should be based on a public plan, requested blocks, milestones, and a rotating resident-staff score, not on bids or personal status, because that is understandable and challengeable; to answer the subjective-scoring objection, the score must use a published rubric with objective indicators and anchors for feasibility, public benefit, and readiness, and written decisions must tie each score to the rubric; this would be contradicted if rubric-governed scoring still proved less understandable or challengeable than opaque bidding without improving project completion.

Unused Project Pool blocks should be progressively released: a milestone check and tentative release to the priority waitlist at 72 hours, a firm release to the Open Pool at 24 hours, and a standby instant-fill queue at start; cancellations should automatically promote waitlisted residents; this would be contradicted if progressive release and standby filling caused more cancellations or no-shows than they cured or still left slots unfilled.

No-show consequences should be small, temporary, and appealable, because permanent exclusion would undermine fairness and challengeability; this would be contradicted if evidence showed that temporary penalties failed to deter no-shows while appeal rights prevented abuse.

A public challenge process with an elected council, a randomly selected resident appeal panel, staff advice, written reasons, and a public log satisfies the requirement that rules be understandable and challengeable, with challenges to project scoring checking rubric application and challenges to release checking timing and standby rules; this would be contradicted if appeals were inaccessible, captured, or unable to correct allocation errors.

Because demand and strategic booking are unknown, the town should run a bounded adaptive trial with pre-announced metrics—newcomer first-use rate, project completion rate, machine utilization, no-show rate, appeal outcomes, bounded access wait time, consecutive-loss rate, urgent-reserve use, unclaimed-reserve return rate, and release fill rate—and adjust only within pre-set bounds; this would be contradicted if adjustments were captured or if fixed rules consistently outperformed adaptive rules under demand shifts.

Therefore the combined arrangement—Open Pool lottery with temporary boosts, bounded access reserve that returns unclaimed blocks to the general draw or standby queue, and consecutive-loss carryover; Project Pool priority by public plan and rubric-scored milestones; progressive release with standby filling; mild appealable no-show penalties; and public bounded review—is the proposed workable allocation; this would be contradicted by a demonstration that the combination systematically fails newcomer fairness, project completion, utilization, or challengeability under plausible demand and strategic response.

fork.earliest_reason: Step 5 is the earliest step that commits to using lottery tickets (with temporary boosts) as the allocation mechanism for the Open Pool, replacing time-priority. This design choice ignores that demand spikes will create periods where lottery odds are low and unpredictable; residents needing emergency repairs or with restrictive schedules may be systematically excluded for weeks despite repeated participation, which a reservation or time-priority hybrid would avoid.
fork.step_quote: The Open Pool should use equal base lottery tickets plus a temporary newcomer or returning-user boost rather than permanent priority, because temporary boosts give newcomers a fair start without creating inherited advantage

objection_text: The Open Pool's pure lottery mechanism assumes equal base tickets suffice for fairness, but when demand is high relative to capacity, a lottery guarantees no minimum access probability for any given week. Residents who need machine access urgently (e.g., for a sudden repair) or who have constrained schedules (e.g., night-shift workers) face repeated low-probability draws with no recourse. The proposal offers no priority queue, reserved emergency slots, or cap on consecutive losses, meaning the arrangement may fail to provide reliable access for non-hobbyist users even as it technically offers 'equal chances.' This defect enters at Step 5 because that is where the commitment to lottery-based allocation for the Open Pool is made, excluding alternative mechanisms that could guarantee bounded wait times or urgent access.
